Electrochemical synthesis routes powered by renewable electricity can provide sustainable chemical
commodities by replacing conventional fossil-based processes. Increasing research focuses on
value-added chemicals like the indispensable fertilizer urea, which also constitutes a study case for
electrochemical CN-coupling. To guide the identiﬁcation of highly selective catalysts, we aim to
provide new insight by analysing existing experimental data on the selectivity of transition metal
catalysts towards electrochemically synthesized urea. Firstly, we project high dimensional
experimental data using principal component analysis (PCA) to lower dimensions, and thereby conﬁrm
that urea selectivity is correlated with the selectivity towards CO and NH3. Furthermore, we identiﬁed
the most suitable two-dimensional descriptors for selectivity prediction out of various adsorption
energies calculated using density functional theory (DFT). We suggest that the adsorption energies of
*H and *O on transition metal slabs predict the selectivity towards urea in the co-reduction of CO2 and
nitrite (NO
2 ).
To mitigate anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions, one of the main
contributing sectors to focus on is the chemical industry, in which ammonia
(NH3) and urea ðCOðNH2Þ2Þ are among the most carbon-intensive
products1–3. This is due to the use of H2 from steam methane reforming to
obtain ammonia in the Haber–Bosch process that operates at 100–400 bar
and 400–650 °C4. Furthermore, urea is derived from ammonia like all other
mineral nitrogen fertilizers: 55% of globally produced ammonia enter urea
production, out of which about 75% are directly used as a fertilizer4.
Therefore, urea has been and will continue to be signiﬁcant for the agri-
cultural productivity apart from further applications as an intermediate
chemicalandinpharmaceuticals5.Conventionally,ureaissynthesizedinthe
thermocatalytic Bosch–Meiser process from CO2 and NH3 under high
pressure and temperatureconditions(150–250bar,100–200°C)5.However,
an electrocatalytic approach to urea synthesis would allow to utilize
increasingly cheap renewable electricity to co-reduce a carbon containing
and nitrogen containing species (CO2 and N2 or NOx∣x∈{1, 2, 3}) to urea.
The electrochemical urea synthesis was studied in the late 1990s by
Shibata et al., and led to their seminal work on electrochemical synthesis of
urea from CO2 and NO

and metallo-phthalocyanines6–11. The associated electrochemical cathodic

Recently, electrochemical urea synthesis has gained more attention,
not least because of being a template reaction for CN-coupling. The range of
successful electrochemical CN-coupling products encompasses other
amines and amides such as methylamine15, glycine16,17, formamide18,19, and
acetamide20,21. The increasing research interest also extends to electro-
chemically synthesized, value-added chemicals that contain CS- and CP-
bonds, with quests for new and improved selective synthetic routes and
catalysts towards C–N, C–S, and C–P products22.
Current research efforts in electrochemical urea synthesis include
catalyst design, e.g. by exploring different catalyst classes, alloying and
vacancy creation23–30. Furthermore, process optimization showed that
pulsed electrolysis can be

a catalyst is highly selective towards urea without referring to a full reaction
mechanism. Therefore, we calculate 10 different adsorption energies for

Correlation with DFT adsorption energies
In order to ﬁnd a predictive atomistic scheme, we calculate adsorption
energies of reaction intermediates to correlate them with experimentally
determined values for FEurea in the co-reduction of NO
2 and CO2 as
reported by Shibata et al. and shown in Fig. 1a9. The 10 adsorption energies
were calculated using DFT (cf. “Computational Details” and the deﬁning
equations are given in the SI) on the 19 transition metals for which
experimental FEurea were available as indicated in Fig. 1a. The most stable
adsorption site for each species on Cu fcc(111) is depicted in Fig. 3a, which
were also the adsorption sites assumed on all the other metals. The calcu-
lated adsorption energies on a metal catalyst M yield each a 10-dimensional
feature vector xM as visualized in Fig. 3b. A PCA on the dataset reduces the
dimension. The ﬁrst and second PC (u1 and u2) building the projection
matrix (U ¼ ½u1; u2T) capture together 95% of the variance in the 19 × 10-
dimensional DFT feature matrix. These original feature vectors for each
metal M are projectedaccording to ½c1;M; c2;MT ¼ UxM, and are marked in
Fig. 3c by ﬁlled circles, where the intensity of red indicates the experimental
FEurea value. From these two-dimensional projections, it is possible to dis-
tinguish the selective catalysts from the ones that do not synthesize urea.
However, it can be also seen that Pd is an outlier in this separation, which
might be due to the calculation of adsorption energies on metallic Pd, while
Pd is known to change to Pd–H under reducing conditions35. To gain
further insight from the PCA, the projection of the original basis vectors, i.e.
the adsorption energies for each adsorbate ΔE*X, are also represented in
Fig. 3c, i.e. in the two-dimensional PCA subspace, in blue, where the crosses
mark the weights ½u1;X; u2;XT of each adsorption energy ΔE*X labeled by
the abbreviation *X.
Among these representations, two subsets, that are each oriented
towards a similar direction, can be identiﬁed: Group 1 consisting of ΔE*O,
ΔE*OH, ΔENO
2, and ΔENO
3; Group 2 consisting of ΔE*H, ΔE*COOH, ΔE*C,
ΔE*CO, ΔE*NO, and ΔE*N. The similar direction of the projected vectors can
be interpreted as a correlation of the adsorption energies within each group
as a result of similar (scaled) weights u1,*X and u2,*X. This can be easily
understood for almost overlapping representations, see e.g. ΔE*OH and
ΔENO
3, which is comparable to the scaling relations between adsorption
energies of molecules binding to a catalyst with the same atomic species36.
When looking more closely at the explained variance plotted per PC in
Fig. S11, not only do the ﬁrst two PCs capture (76 + 19)% = 95%, but also
can we see that 100% is reached with ﬁve PCs, where the third to ﬁfth PC
each add only 1–2 percentage points. Therefore, it is concluded that the
adsorption energies can be projected into a two-dimensional orthogonal
basis without signiﬁcant loss of information. In other words, the most
distinguishing trend of the adsorption energies on the different metal cat-
alysts can be described by choosing two representative adsorption energies,
which are orthogonal in our PCA plot. While most adsorption energies
group very clearly, such that they can be represented by a multiple of one
representative out of each group, the adsorption energies ΔE*N, and ΔE*NO
do not group perfectly. However, they can still be captured by a linear
combination of two orthogonal descriptors due to the high explained var-
iance in the two-dimensional principal subspace.
We choose here the almost orthogonal adsorption energies ΔE*H and
ΔE*O as representative adsorption energies, that are meaningful and
interpretable descriptors: The choice of ΔE*H from group 2 as a descriptor is
motivated by its classifying property for the selectivity in electrochemical
CO2 electroreduction37. ΔE*H is approximately scaling linearly with the
other species of group 2 that bind with a carbon or nitrogen atom to the
catalyst surface (cf. Fig. S7). On the other hand, all adsorbates out of group 1
are binding through an oxygen atom and their adsorption energies are
linearly correlated as it can be seen in Fig. S6. Therefore, similar results are
obtained if any other second descriptor from group 1 is chosen instead of
ΔE*O as shown in Fig. S5. To furtherstrengthen the case for the suitability of
the descriptorΔE*O:CuZn-catalysts have beenshown to perform selectively
in electrochemical urea synthesis26,27, while CuZn has also been identiﬁed as
an active methanol synthesis catalyst based on the descriptor ΔE*O
38,39.

Conclusion
One of the persisting challenges in the progression towards electrochemical
synthesis routes for value-added products is the selectivity of a catalyst.

In this work, we demonstrate that a predictive scheme for selectivity
towards urea on transition metals in the co-reduction of CO2 and NO
2 can
be obtained based on a two-dimensional descriptor. In the ﬁrst part of this
work, we presented an analysis of existing experimental data in literature
and showed the correlation of the faradaic efﬁciency towards urea FEurea
with FECO and FENH3 by employingprinciple component analysisto reduce
the nine-dimensional experimental data points that were digitized from the
seminal work of Shibata et al.6–8. At the same time, we also found that there
might be freedom in the choice of experimental conditions to decouple the
dependency of FEurea. In the second part, we suggested ultimately a two-
dimensional descriptor based on our setof 10 considered descriptors, which
are adsorption energies calculated using DFT on 19 different transition
metal catalysts. After applying PCA, we could conclude that the adsorption
energy of *O (ΔE*O) and the adsorption energy of *H (ΔE*H) can explain
the trends in another set of experimental data for FEurea starting from the
same reactants as before9. We found that selectivity towards urea is corre-
lated with small, but positive adsorption energies ΔE*H while oxygen
binding should be as strong as possible in the range of investigated ΔE*O.
Interestingly, this also explains why CuZn works so well for urea
synthesis26,27; Zn is very oxophilic (strong *O binding) and Cu is good at
providing CO at moderate *H binding.
Methods
Computational details: DFT
All DFT calculations were carried out using the Atomic Simulation Envir-
onment (ASE)40 and the GPAW calculator41 in plane wave mode using the
RPBE exchange-correlation functional42 with an energy convergence tol-
erance of 1 × 10−4 eV. For the determination of the lattice constant, bulk fcc
structureswererelaxedwithamaximalremainingforceof1×10−2 eVÅ−1,a
cut-off energy of 800 eV and a k-point grid of 10 × 10 × 10. The thereby
obtainedlatticeconstantwasthenusedtodeﬁnefcc(111)3×4×4slabswith
two ﬁxed bottom layers (four ﬁxed layers for Co, Cr, Mo, Mn and Ni). The
DFT energy for the clean slabs and adsorbateswere calculated with a cut-off
energy of 500 eV, a force criterion of at least 5 × 10−2 eV Å−1 and a 4 × 3 × 1
k-point sampling grid. Spin-polarized calculations were used for the Co, Ni,
Cr and Mn slabs with the ﬁrst two being ferromagnetic and the last two
antiferromagnetic. The total energies of the reference gases, that are needed
to calculate adsorption energies according to the equations stated below and
in the SI, were determined with a cut-off energy of 500 eV (same cut-off as
for the adsorbate systems), a 1 × 1 × 1 k-point grid and a maximal force of
1 × 10−2 eV Å−1.
The most stable site for each adsorbed species among the possible sites
on a fcc(111) plane (i.e. on top, bridge, fcc, hcp) were determined on Cu and
used for all other metals, too. These most stable sites associated with lowest
DFT energy among the considered sites are shown in Fig. 3a.
In the following three paragraphs, we are providing additional support
for our assumption of ﬁrstly, using fcc structures to model all metals, sec-
ondly, using the most stable site on Cu fcc(111) for the adsorbates on all
metals, and thirdly, of using only the fcc(111) facet instead of a stepped one.
The ﬁrst simpliﬁcation is that in fact, not all of the considered metals are
commonly occurring in a fcc crystal structure at room temperature43.
Therefore, for bcc and hcp structures, we calculated all 10 adsorption
energies on the respective closed packed facet, i.e. bcc(110) for Cr, and Mo;
hcp(0001) for Cd, Co, Ru, Tl, and Zn. For bcc(110) and hcp(0001), all
standard sites (i.e. {on top, long bridge, short bridge, hollow} and {on top,
